rv.q: Jordan Fein’s magical production of Sondheim and James Lapine’s fairytale meta-mash-up is even better than ever.
It’s just great, really, a sublime production of a sublime musical with a sublime cast.

This immaculate revival at the Bridge Theatre shows why: done well, it needs a huge, and hugely capable, cast to sing the fiendish staccato score, as well as trees, cows, giants, witches, magic, humour, horror and heart.
It's hard to imagine a production that does a better job of tying all the themes and subthemes together and actually making you care about the characters as they confront the darkness in Act Two.
It is hard to imagine a more thrilling rendition.
Fein and Scutt’s supernaturally good mix of the dark and the light ensures its spell never breaks.
Fein and co have treated this musical with the care and seriousness it deserves – and that’s a spell not easily broken.

Jordan Fein's revival of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine's musical mash–up of the Brothers' fairy tales is an absolute hoot – gorgeously dressed and designed by Tom Scutt and bottling all their stories' subversive enchantment.
Jordan Fein’s production shimmers and shines with all the humour and pathos of these errant fairytale characters who misadventure into the woods, winding their rearranged stories around each other.
This musical has an unmistakably elegant froideur about it, making it easier to admire than love.

The honour now falls to another American director, Olivier Award-winner Jordan Fein, whose beautiful production for the Bridge Theatre makes a classy alternative to panto yet is richly detailed enough long to outlive the festive season.
This production is very Fein indeed.
Fein’s production looks and sounds sumptuous, yet it’s a little like an expensive chocolate box, with nothing within that offers any fresh or surprising flavour.
This is a much darker, sexier and more thrilling journey into the woods than I’ve ever experienced before.
A celebration of these twisted fairytales, this is a razor-sharp production full of heart, thoughtful design and wonderful performances.
A production that has lost none of its magic.
It’s a great production of a terrific show.
Fein has created a production that has magic and drama, danger and hope, and is sinister and illusory all at once.
This is not merely an outstanding revival of a musical masterpiece.
This return to the woods is not to be missed.

Does this first-rate production thrive in its new West End home? The jewel box Noël Coward Theatre, with its gilt-speckled Rococo-style interior, is a good match for Sondheim's satirical fairy tale where wishes can come true.
For anyone yet to experience this iconic musical, this production honours the heart of Into the Woods while offering a subtle, cohesive and wholly absorbing version.
Into the Woods manages to be both very funny and moving, often at the same time.
Into the Woods, let's dare to state it, is the most perfect music-theatre creation of the last 40 years.

Dominic Cavendish thought this production was “a classy alternative to panto yet is richly detailed enough long to outlive the festive season.” He wrote, “A plot that could easily become convoluted is instead brisk and hypnotic.” He found Scutt’s set design impressive in evoking the magical woodland scene.

The method of delivery is too delightfully silly to resist, and a new revival of “Into the Woods,” at the Bridge Theater in London through May 30, makes the most of the musical’s whimsical premise, leaning into the visuals of fairy tale lore with a spirit of winking pastiche.
Jordan Fein's direction has injected humour and charm into the musical with a few necessary twists of the macabre.
All things considered, it’s a very satisfying and gritty show, with touches of lighthearted silliness in amongst the doom and gloom.
But this is not an extraordinary production.
Where the 2007. Linbury production charmed and the 2010. Regent’s Park staging impressed, the Bridge Theatre’s Into the Woods soars.
This revival at The Bridge is one of the most magical shows of the year: a fairy-tale evening that balances spectacle with bite.
It’s theatre at its absolute finest.
It is a stirring and stunning production that I am proud to say has survived its transfer, and truly is, in my opinion, a perfect production of a perfect musical.
This adaptation is a triumphant and an other-worldly return for the much-loved musical, one that truly honours the intentions of the original.
An unforgettable show that I wouldn't even hesitate in giving 5 stars to, not one moment of hesitation at all.
This is a fabulous, maximalist way to see Sondheim, with a great ensemble and an even greater creative team.
Into the Woods is a masterful production, trusting its script, performers and audience, resulting in a production for the ages.

Transferring from the wide open spaces of the Bridge Theatre to the more traditional end-on setting of a traditional proscenium arch theatre like the Noël Coward has resulted in a tighter, funnier and ultimately even more satisfying production of Into the Woods.
It’s thoughtful, emotionally intelligent, visually beautiful, and full of heart.
The evening is a constellation of talents.
This magnificent revival directed by Jordan Fein is as black as a politician’s soul, as icy as their hearts.
For Sondheim-obsessives, it might be even more of a treat: a chance to see one of the great composer’s classic pieces produced well, produced honestly, and produced seemingly without ego.
It’s the perfect adaptation of Sondheim’s masterpiece, feeling nostalgic and true without feeling repetitive of its previous iterations.
Theatre’s revival of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine’s masterpiece was magnificent.
But Fein, always true to emotion, never lets you forget that he’s in the entertainment business.
Fein’s respectful, conscientious, approach makes it a sure hit as well as a true pleasure.
Ultimately, I found this a refreshing and accomplished take on a beloved musical.
This production of Into the Woods is playing at The Bridge until May.
The cast crawl, climb, leap and tumble across Tom Scutt's set, which is nothing short of magical: tall, untamed grass and towering trees that transport the audience straight into the forest.
These are woods you’ll want to get lost in; just remember to drop your breadcrumbs.
Moments in the woods will surely make the children listen.
So grab a ticket, musical fans - or face an unhappy ending.
The Woods is an incredible must see show!
Jordan Fein's production succeeds in capturing the complexity of this musical that makes it so enduring.
The Woods is a visually thrilling treat with Christmas parallels but which could be viewed at any time of year boasting an exquisite cast singing some of Sondheim's most affecting work.
The combination of gorgeous design and stunning individual performances is effective in crafting a memorable production, forming a final package that is as magical as the characters that live there.
This version of Into the Woods is simple yet stylish, which is perhaps is the perfect way to honour Sondheim who could say so much with so few words.
This is a predatory place in which survival means you must learn that the forest is no place for dreaming.
Very uneven in its approach, when it is good, it is extremely good, but other moments fail to match the standard and promise seen elsewhere.
What’s conflicting, then, is that this particular staging is fine
This is an astonishing piece of theatre that highlights every note, cadence and inflection of Sondheim’s extraordinary score.
Simply stunning from start to finish.
Audiences may not find themselves home before dark on the ever-shortening days, but what remains is a journey of a musical epic that continues to thrill.
For fans of Sondheim musicals, this production of Into The Woods would certainly be one to go and see.

While there are moments of enjoyment scattered throughout the woods, this revival is safer than a vault at Gringotts and ultimately represents a giant missed opportunity to create something truly magical.

cn.t: Jordan Fein's Olivier-winning revival earns near-universal acclaim for its magical staging and emotional depth. Critics hail it as a thrilling, intimate production that perfectly balances Sondheim's dark wit with poignant storytelling.
